title: Latency vs throughput vs bandwidth
scopeHtml:
Scope: definitions, Little's law, utilisation, percentiles, tail latency, latency reduction.

Scope: definitions, Little's law, utilisation, percentiles, tail latency, latency reduction.

notes.title: Latency, throughput and bandwidth
notes.html:
Latency is how long ONE request takes. Throughput is how many requests finish per second. Bandwidth is the maximum data the pipe can carry per second. They are different and often confused.

Think of a motorway: latency is the time one car takes from A to B, throughput is cars arriving per minute, bandwidth is the number of lanes times speed limit (the capacity).

Latency    = time for one request      (ms)
Throughput = completed requests / time (req/s, or MB/s of useful data)
Bandwidth  = max capacity of the link  (Mbps / Gbps)
Throughput <= Bandwidth (on a link); latency is not bandwidth

Worked example. A 1 Gbps link has about 125 MB/s of bandwidth. Sending a 1 KB response takes 8 microseconds to push onto the wire, but a round trip to another continent still costs 150 ms. More bandwidth does NOT fix latency; a faster pipe does not make light travel faster.

Industry examples. Satellite internet (geostationary) has decent bandwidth but 500+ ms latency. Starlink targets tens of ms by using low orbit. CDNs (Cloudflare, Akamai) reduce latency by moving content closer, not by widening links.

Everyday analogy. Water pipe: bandwidth is the pipe's width, latency is how long the first drop takes to arrive, throughput is litres per minute actually coming out.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "we need more bandwidth" for a latency problem.
  • Quoting throughput of a system without the latency at that load.
  • Mixing Mbps (bits) with MB/s (bytes), a factor of 8.

notes.title: How latency and throughput relate: Little's law
notes.html:
Little's law: concurrent requests in the system L = throughput lambda x average latency W. It lets you size thread pools, connection pools and queues.

Worked example. An API handles 2,000 req/s with 50 ms average latency. In flight: 2,000 x 0.05 = 100 concurrent requests. A thread pool of 50 will queue; a pool of 200 is comfortable. If the database slows and latency goes to 500 ms at the same arrival rate, in flight becomes 1,000, which exhausts pools and cascades. That is how a slow dependency becomes an outage.

Production symptom. Latency climbs, thread/connection pool "active" count hits its max, queue depth grows, then timeouts. The metric to graph: in-flight requests (or pool saturation) next to p99.

Industry examples. HikariCP's docs advise small DB pools (often about 10 to 20 per app instance) because more connections than the DB can run in parallel only add queueing. Postgres commonly needs PgBouncer when hundreds of app instances each hold connections.

Everyday analogy. A coffee shop: 2 customers per minute arriving, each taking 3 minutes at the barista, means 6 people are inside at any moment.

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing a pool by guesswork instead of rate x latency.
  • Forgetting that latency rises as utilisation approaches 100% (next section).

notes.title: Why latency explodes near full utilisation
notes.html:
A queue grows without bound as utilisation approaches 100%. For a simple single-server queue, average wait grows like 1 / (1 - utilisation).

Utilisation   1/(1-u)   Relative to 50%
50%           2         1x
80%           5         2.5x
90%           10        5x
95%           20        10x
99%           100       50x

Decision gravity. Target 50 to 70% peak utilisation on stateless tiers. Running hot saves money but turns small spikes into timeouts; this is reversible (add servers) if autoscaling is fast, a trap if scaling takes 10 minutes.

Worked example. Service at 600 ms p99 sits at 90% CPU. Adding 30% more servers drops CPU to about 70% and p99 to 150 ms with no code change.

Industry examples. Google SRE guidance and Netflix autoscaling policies aim for headroom (often 50 to 60% target CPU). Load shedding (rejecting excess early) is used by many large services to protect latency of accepted requests.

Everyday analogy. A motorway at 95% capacity: one slow lorry causes a jam that lasts an hour.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing latency grows linearly with load.
  • Sizing to the average, not peak, and with no headroom.

notes.title: Percentiles: p50, p95, p99
notes.html:
Averages hide pain. Use percentiles. p99 = 99% of requests are faster than this value, so 1 in 100 is slower.

1000 requests sorted by latency:
p50 (median) = 500th value  -> typical user
p95          = 950th value
p99          = 990th value  -> the unlucky 1%
p99.9        = 999th value
max          = worst case

Worked example. 98 requests at 50 ms and 2 requests at 2,000 ms: average = (98x50 + 2x2000)/100 = 89 ms (looks fine), p50 = 50 ms, p99 = 2,000 ms. A user making 20 requests per page view has a 1 - 0.99^20 = 18% chance of hitting at least one slow request. So p99 matters for page experience, not just 1% of users.

Rule: never average percentiles across machines. The p99 of the fleet is NOT the mean of each host's p99. Aggregate histograms (for example Prometheus histogram buckets, HdrHistogram) instead.

Industry examples. Amazon reports SLAs at p99.9; Google's search tracks tail latency heavily. Prometheus histogram_quantile and HdrHistogram are the common tools. Datadog and Grafana show p50/p95/p99 by default.

Decision gravity. Choosing which percentile is the SLO is a business contract: p99 vs p99.9 changes cost a lot because each extra 9 needs more capacity, hedging and isolation.

Everyday analogy. A school class average mark can be 70 while a few students fail badly.

Common interview traps.

  • Reporting only average latency.
  • Averaging p99s across servers.
  • Using too few samples; p99.9 needs thousands of requests per window.

notes.title: Tail latency amplification
notes.html:
When one request fans out to N backends, the slowest one decides the total. If each backend is slow 1% of the time, the chance at least one of 100 is slow is 1 - 0.99^100 = 63%.

Mitigations:

  • Hedged requests: send a duplicate to another replica after the p95 time; take the first answer. Costs about 5% more load, cuts tail a lot (Google's "Tail at Scale" paper).
  • Timeouts and partial results: return what you have by 200 ms.
  • Reduce fan-out: fewer shards per query, caching, better partitioning.
  • Isolate noisy neighbours and avoid GC pauses (tune heap, use G1/ZGC).

Worked example. Search over 100 shards, each with p99 = 100 ms. Without mitigation roughly 63% of queries wait about 100 ms or more. With a hedge at 20 ms the slow outliers shrink to the order of 30 ms for little extra load.

Industry examples. Google search, Elasticsearch (adaptive replica selection), Cassandra (speculative retry), DynamoDB clients.

Everyday analogy. A group dinner: everyone waits for the slowest dish.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring fan-out when computing end-to-end p99.
  • Retrying blindly (no cap), which turns hedging into a retry storm.

notes.title: Where latency comes from and how to cut it
notes.html:
Break an end-to-end request into stages and measure each. Typical budget for a mobile API call: DNS 20 ms, TCP+TLS 100 to 150 ms on first connect, server 50 ms, DB 10 ms, download 30 ms.

Cuts, in the usual order of payoff:

  1. Do less: cache, avoid N+1 queries, fewer round trips (batch).
  2. Move closer: CDN, edge, regional deployment.
  3. Reuse connections: HTTP keep-alive, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 (QUIC), connection pools.
  4. Do in parallel and async: fan out independent calls, queue non-critical work.
  5. Compress and shrink payloads (gzip/brotli, protobuf, image sizes).

Worked example (Android). Feed screen made 6 sequential calls at 120 ms = 720 ms. Combining into one aggregate call and caching the unchanged parts in Room gives 150 ms for a network refresh and an instant (0 ms) render from cache.

Industry examples. Facebook GraphQL, Netflix's API aggregation (BFF pattern) reduce mobile round trips. Cloudflare and Google use QUIC to cut handshake time.

Throughput levers (separate from latency): batching, pipelining, more partitions and workers, async I/O, larger buffers. Batching raises throughput but often adds latency (the wait to fill a batch); Kafka producers tune linger.ms and batch.size for this trade-off.

Decision gravity. Batching/async trade-offs are reversible config; adding a cache layer adds an invalidation problem that is hard to remove later.

Everyday analogy. Reducing a commute: shorter route, avoid traffic, travel in parallel lanes.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising throughput when the SLO is latency, or the reverse.
  • Forgetting first-connection costs (DNS, TLS) in mobile.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Latency = time per request; throughput = requests per second; bandwidth = pipe capacity. More bandwidth does not cut latency.
  • Little's law: in flight = rate x latency; use it to size pools and spot cascades.
  • Latency rises sharply above 70 to 80% utilisation; keep headroom.
  • Use percentiles (p50/p95/p99), never averages; do not average p99s.
  • Fan-out amplifies the tail; use hedging, timeouts, fewer shards.
  • Cut latency by doing less, moving closer, reusing connections, parallelising; batching trades latency for throughput.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between latency, throughput and bandwidth? A teammate says "the API is slow, let's buy a bigger network pipe". Is that right?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who mix these three measures size systems wrongly. It is the first filter on whether you can reason about performance.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many requests complete per second. Bandwidth is the maximum the pipe can carry per second. A bigger pipe raises the ceiling on throughput but does nothing for the time one request takes, because that is dominated by distance, handshakes and server work. So I would measure first, and only buy bandwidth if the link is actually saturated.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Latency    = time for ONE request            (ms)
Throughput = completed work / time           (req/s, MB/s)
Bandwidth  = max capacity of the link        (Mbps, Gbps)
On a link: throughput <= bandwidth. Latency is a separate axis.

A 1 Gbps link is about 125 MB/s (divide bits by 8). A 1 KB response takes about 8 microseconds to serialise onto that wire, but a round trip to another continent costs about 150 ms because light in fibre is the limit. Making the pipe 10x wider changes the 8 microseconds to 0.8 microseconds and the 150 ms not at all. Satellite internet in geostationary orbit has fine bandwidth and 500+ ms latency; a CDN helps by moving content closer, not by widening links.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "more bandwidth" for a latency problem.
  • Quoting throughput without the latency at that load.
  • Mixing Mbps (bits) with MB/s (bytes), a factor of 8.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When does bandwidth become the bottleneck? -> Large payloads (video, bulk export, backups) or a saturated link: throughput flatlines at link capacity and queueing latency rises.
  2. Can high throughput coexist with high latency? -> Yes, a satellite link or a batch pipeline moves lots of data with long per-item delay.
  3. How do you improve latency for users on another continent? -> Move work closer (CDN, regional deployment), reuse connections to skip repeated handshakes, cut round trips.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer defines the three words. The senior asks which one the SLO is about, measures per-stage time (DNS, TLS, server, DB) and shows that the proposed fix moves the dominant stage.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams have paid for bigger links and seen no change because the time was in sequential cross-region calls.

questions.promptHtml: State Little's law and show how you would use it to size a thread pool.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the cheapest piece of math that turns "latency went up" into "the pool is exhausted".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Requests in flight equals arrival rate times average time in the system: L = lambda x W. If I serve 2,000 req/s at 50 ms average, 100 requests are in flight at any moment, so I need at least about 100 workers, and I add headroom. If latency rises to 500 ms at the same rate, 1,000 are in flight and a pool of 200 is exhausted. That is how a slow dependency turns into an outage.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
L = lambda x W
2000 req/s x 0.050 s  = 100 in flight
2000 req/s x 0.500 s  = 1000 in flight

It holds for any stable system regardless of distribution, so it applies to threads, DB connections, queue depth. Use the latency measured at the dependency you are sizing for, not at the edge. For DB pools the answer is usually smaller than people expect: connections beyond what the DB can run in parallel only add queueing, which is why HikariCP docs suggest small pools (often 10 to 20 per instance; verify for your DB).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
rate, latency = 2000, 0.050
in_flight = rate * latency      # 100
pool = int(in_flight * 1.5)     # 50% headroom -> 150

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sizing pools by gut feel instead of rate x latency.
  • Using average latency when sizing for a tail (use p95 for headroom).
  • Forgetting that latency itself rises as the pool fills.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do you graph next to p99? -> In-flight count or pool saturation; they move together.
  2. Does it need exponential arrivals? -> No, only a stable system in steady state.
  3. A downstream slows 10x at constant arrival rate, what happens? -> In flight grows 10x, pools exhaust, queues grow, timeouts trigger retries which add rate: cascade.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: states the formula. Senior: uses it to explain a cascade and to choose a pool, timeout and queue limit together.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The standard shape of a "database got slow, whole site went down" incident.

questions.promptHtml: Why do we report p99 rather than the average, and why is averaging p99 across servers wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Wrong aggregation is the most common bug in dashboards and SLO reports.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The average hides the slow minority. With 98 requests at 50 ms and 2 at 2,000 ms the average is 89 ms but p99 is 2,000 ms. Users make many requests per page, so the tail hits more than 1% of them. And you cannot average per-host p99s because a percentile is not linear; you merge histograms, then compute the percentile on the merged data.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A page view with 20 requests has 1 - 0.99^20 = 18% chance of hitting a p99-slow call. Percentiles come from sorted samples (p99 = the value 99% of requests beat). Host A with 10 req/s and host B with 10,000 req/s: the mean of their p99s weights them equally, which is wrong. Prometheus histogram buckets are additive, so histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(x_bucket[5m]))) merges before computing. HdrHistogram does the same offline. Sample count matters: p99.9 over a window with 500 requests is basically the max.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Average latency alone on dashboards.
  • avg(p99) across instances.
  • p99.9 on too few samples.
  • Client-side coordinated omission in load tests (slow responses suppress the next sends).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which percentile should the SLO use? -> The one matching user pain and cost: p99 for most, p99.9 only if the business pays, since each extra 9 needs hedging and isolation.
  2. Can you add two percentiles? -> No; only histograms/sketches merge.
  3. Why does p99 of a page exceed p99 of each call? -> Fan-out; the page waits for the slowest of N calls.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "average is misleading". Senior: shows the arithmetic, names the aggregation rule, and ties the percentile choice to cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Dashboards showing a healthy fleet-wide p99 while one noisy host timed out for its users.

questions.contextHtml: An order service peaks at 1,500 req/s. Each request calls Postgres once; DB time is 20 ms average, 80 ms p95. The service runs on 6 pods, each with a HikariCP pool of 100, so 600 connections. The Postgres primary has 16 vCPUs and max_connections = 500. During peak, DB CPU is 85% and p99 is 900 ms. A colleague says "raise the pool to 200 per pod, we are waiting on connections".
questions.promptHtml: Do you agree? How would you size the pools?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Agrees to raise pool size because threads are "waiting for a connection". It would also exceed max_connections and push the DB from queueing at the app to queueing inside the DB, which is worse.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 20 ms DB time measured at the DB or at the client (includes wait)? Are the connections idle or active? Is the DB CPU bound? Any other clients of this DB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not raise pools. If errors are present, shed non-critical load or scale read paths away.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) DB CPU saturated so more connections only add contention; (b) a few slow queries holding connections; (c) pool too large causing context-switch overhead; (d) red herring: network, DB time is small.
  4. How I'd verify each: Little's law: 1,500 x 0.020 = 30 connections busy on average, at p95 1,500 x 0.080 = 120. So about 30 to 120 active connections are enough; 600 is 5 to 20x more than needed. Check pg_stat_activity for active vs idle, and EXPLAIN the slow queries.
  5. Root cause: DB CPU at 85% means we are in the 1/(1-u) region; queueing happens at the DB regardless of pool size.
  6. Fix: Short term: shrink to about 20 per pod (120 total) and put PgBouncer in transaction mode if instance count grows. Long term: index or cache the heavy queries, read replicas, add DB CPU headroom.
  7. Prevention: Alert on pool wait time and DB active connections, not just pool size.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise max_connections; each Postgres backend costs memory and scheduling overhead.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Autoscaling doubles pods at peak? -> Total connections double: a fixed per-pod pool breaks, so cap globally with PgBouncer.
  • Latency target is 100 ms, not 900? -> Reduce DB utilisation below about 60% first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team tripled pool size during an incident and turned slow responses into a full DB lockup; shrinking the pool and adding an index fixed it in an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises the pool.
  • Hire: computes in-flight with Little's law and shrinks.
  • Strong hire: adds PgBouncer, global connection budget, and the DB-side queueing explanation.

questions.contextHtml:
Dashboard panel "API p99" shows 180 ms and green. Support reports checkout timeouts for some users. The panel query:

avg(
  histogram_quantile(0.99,
    rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[5m]))
)

There are 12 pods. Eleven serve 800 req/s each at p99 = 150 ms. One pod in a bad zone serves 40 req/s at p99 = 2.4 s.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with the panel and what is the real fleet p99?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The average is hiding the outlier", without fixing aggregation or noting that the bad pod has little traffic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are all buckets the same across pods? Is there per-pod and per-zone labelling? Do the timeouts correlate with a zone?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drain or restart the bad pod; check its zone.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Query bug (certain), plus a real bad pod (noisy neighbour, bad node).
  4. How I'd verify: The panel computes (11 x 150 + 2400)/12 = 337 ms, not 180, but it also weights the slow pod as 1/12 while it serves under 0.5% of traffic. Correct query:
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="api"}[5m])))
  1. Root cause: percentiles are not linear; averaging gives a number that is no percentile of anything.
  2. Fix: merge buckets with sum by (le); add a per-pod/zone panel to find outliers; alert on the merged p99 and on per-instance outliers separately.
  3. Prevention: Review rule: no avg() or max() wrapped around histogram_quantile.
  4. Trade-offs: Merged p99 is dominated by busy pods, so a small bad pod can still hide; hence the per-pod view.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is the merged p99 still fine while users complain? -> The bad pod serves under 1% of traffic, so it sits above p99; try p99.9 or a user-journey SLI.
  • Buckets are too coarse? -> The quantile interpolates within a bucket; add buckets near the SLO threshold.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet showed green for weeks while one availability zone had a failing NIC; per-zone latency panels found it in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "use p95 instead".
  • Hire: sums buckets before the quantile.
  • Strong hire: also adds per-instance outlier detection and notes traffic weighting.

questions.contextHtml: Product says: "The app feels slow for our users in Brazil. Make it faster." The API is deployed only in a US region. Server-side p50 is 40 ms. Brazil users see 900 ms to first data on a cold app start, 450 ms on later calls. The mobile client opens a fresh HTTPS connection per call. Budget: one engineer-month.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Jumps to "add a CDN" or "buy more servers" without measuring what the 900 ms is made of.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the target (p75 first data under 500 ms)? Which screens? Is the data user-specific or cacheable? Do we have real-user monitoring by country?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is a performance project, so first measure.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Round trips dominate: Brazil to US is roughly 120 to 150 ms RTT (verify). A fresh connection costs DNS + TCP + TLS 1.2 = about 3 round trips before the first byte, so about 400 ms of pure setup. Server work is only 40 ms.
  4. How I'd verify: RUM breakdown or a curl timing run from Brazil: curl -w "dns:%{time_namelookup} connect:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer}\n".
  5. Root cause: Handshakes and sequential calls times RTT, not server speed.
  6. Fix: In order of payoff: reuse connections (keep-alive, HTTP/2, TLS 1.3 / HTTP/3 to cut handshakes), batch the cold-start calls into one, cache static and semi-static responses locally, then CDN or an edge for cacheable APIs, then a regional deployment (costly, adds data replication; a one-way-ish door).
  7. Prevention: Track p75 by country in RUM.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a second region first; it is the most expensive lever and the data layer becomes multi-region.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• All data is per-user and uncacheable? -> Then fewer round trips and connection reuse matter even more; consider edge termination for TLS.
  • 10 ms server time saved? -> Invisible next to 400 ms of handshakes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team spent a quarter tuning queries before a per-stage trace showed 70% of cold-start time was three sequential TLS handshakes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale servers.
  • Hire: breaks down by stage and reuses connections.
  • Strong hire: orders levers by cost and reversibility and defines the target metric.

questions.promptHtml: Why does latency shoot up when a service runs at 90 to 95% utilisation even though it still has capacity left?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who size for the average from those who understand queues.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Requests arrive randomly, so sometimes several arrive together. At low utilisation the server clears the burst quickly. Near full utilisation there is no spare capacity to drain the queue, so waiting time grows roughly like 1/(1-u): 5x at 80%, 10x at 90%, 20x at 95%. So I keep peak utilisation around 50 to 70% on latency-sensitive tiers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
u      1/(1-u)
50%    2
80%    5
90%    10
95%    20
99%    100

This is the single-server queueing shape (M/M/1); real systems differ in constants but not in the knee. Burstiness, garbage collection and noisy neighbours make it worse. A queue that grows faster than it drains keeps growing, so one slow second at 95% becomes a minute of backlog. Autoscaling is reactive and takes minutes, so the headroom has to exist before the spike.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking latency is linear in load.
  • Sizing to average load with no peak margin.
  • Trusting CPU alone: queues also form at locks, pools and disks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you protect latency when overloaded anyway? -> Load shedding: reject early, bounded queues, so accepted requests stay fast.
  2. Why 50 to 70% and not 90%? -> Cost of an extra server vs timeouts during spikes; depends on how fast you can scale.
  3. Is the knee the same for a multi-core server? -> It moves later (more servers sharing one queue) but still exists.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it gets slow when busy". Senior: gives the 1/(1-u) table, picks a utilisation target from scaling speed, and proposes shedding.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Services "fine at 60% CPU" that fall over at the first traffic spike once autoscaling lag is included.

questions.contextHtml: Finance wants to cut cloud cost 25% on the stateless search-API tier: 20 servers, autoscaling target CPU 50%, peak CPU observed 60%, p99 120 ms. A proposal raises the autoscaling target to 85% so the fleet shrinks to about 12 servers. Autoscaling needs about 4 minutes to add capacity. Traffic spikes of +40% in 1 minute happen weekly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Approves because CPU at 85% is "still under 100%" with no thought for queueing or scaling lag.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the latency SLO? How spiky is the traffic? Is cost the only driver? Can we use a mix of scheduled and reactive scaling?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; this is a change review.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The saving is real but the risk is the knee: 1/(1-0.6) = 2.5 vs 1/(1-0.85) = 6.7, so queueing delay is about 2.7x worse before spikes.
  4. How I'd verify: Load test at 85% and at 85% x 1.4 = 119% (overload). Replay last month's spike.
  5. Root cause of the risk: A +40% spike in 1 minute at 85% pushes demand past capacity for about 3 minutes while the scale-out catches up: unbounded queues and timeouts.
  6. Fix: Compromise: target 65 to 70% (about 15 servers, 25% saving with a smaller hit), add scheduled scale-up before known peaks, load shedding and bounded queues, faster scale-out (warm pool).
  7. Prevention: SLO-based alert so we see budget burn after the change.
  8. Trade-offs: The change is reversible in hours, which makes a staged trial fine: try 70% for two weeks and watch p99 and error budget.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Spikes were smoother? -> Higher target becomes acceptable.
  • Reserved instances instead? -> Cost lever independent of utilisation; discuss it first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet right-sized to 85% looked great for a month, then a marketing email produced a spike; four minutes of timeouts cost more than the year's savings.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves.
  • Hire: shows queueing math and proposes 65 to 70%.
  • Strong hire: includes scale-out lag, shedding, staged rollout.

questions.contextHtml:
03:12: alert "checkout 5xx > 5%". Checkout runs 30 pods with 100 Tomcat threads each (3,000 threads) at 2,000 req/s, normally 50 ms. Recently a promo service the checkout calls (non-critical) was deployed. Metrics:

checkout p50 50ms -> 6.2s ; thread pool active 3000/3000 ; queue 4812
promo-svc p50 40ms -> 6.0s ; promo-svc cpu 8%
db p99 12ms (unchanged)  ; checkout cpu 15%

The HTTP client to promo-svc has no timeout configured. Checkout is not CPU bound.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and how you handle it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames checkout CPU or the DB (red herrings), scales checkout pods, which just adds more threads blocked on the same dependency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in promo-svc and when? Is promo-svc hung or slow? Is checkout the only caller? Is there a feature flag for promo?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Flip the flag to skip promo (it is optional) or fail fast; roll back promo-svc.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) promo-svc slow plus no client timeout; (b) promo-svc deadlock/GC; (c) DB: ruled out (12 ms, CPU low).
  4. How I'd verify: jstack shows threads in socketRead on promo-svc; promo-svc thread dump; compare the deploy time with onset.
  5. Root cause: Little's law: 2,000 req/s x 6 s = 12,000 in flight against 3,000 threads. Pools saturate and the queue grows, so everything slow shows as 5xx. Checkout CPU is low because threads are blocked, not working.
  6. Fix: Short term: flag off, rollback. Long term: timeout on every client call (for example 200 ms for an optional dependency), a bulkhead (separate pool for promo), a circuit breaker with fallback "no promo", mark promo optional.
  7. Prevention: Lint rule that fails clients without a timeout; chaos test injecting latency into optional dependencies; alert on pool saturation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not scaling checkout, not raising thread count; more threads only raise memory and the blast.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Promo must be shown at checkout (not optional)? -> Cache last known promos with a TTL as fallback; degrade to static banner.
  • Why did CPU stay at 15%? -> Threads blocked on I/O do no CPU work.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An "optional" recommendation widget with an infinite timeout took down a payment flow because it shared the request thread pool.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales pods.
  • Hire: finds the missing timeout and sheds promo.
  • Strong hire: computes in-flight, adds bulkhead and breaker, writes a prevention lint.

questions.contextHtml: Product search queries 20 shards today; each shard has p99 = 80 ms, p50 = 10 ms. Next quarter the index grows 5x and the plan is 100 shards. SLO: p95 end-to-end under 120 ms. A proposal to meet it: "retry any shard call that has not returned in 100 ms, up to 3 times, at every layer (client, aggregator, shard proxy)".
questions.promptHtml: Estimate the impact of going from 20 to 100 shards and critique the retry proposal.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Shards are fast, so end-to-end will be fast", and approves retries without computing the multiplication.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we return partial results? Are replicas available per shard? Is the query read-only (safe to duplicate)? Can fan-out be reduced by routing?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; design review.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Fan-out amplification dominates: chance at least one shard hits its p99 is 1 - 0.99^20 = 18% today and 1 - 0.99^100 = 63% at 100 shards.
  4. How I'd verify: Load test with injected slow shard responses; measure end-to-end p95.
  5. Root cause: The whole query waits for the slowest shard, so end-to-end p95 approaches the per-shard p99 once the fan-out is large.
  6. Fix: Hedged requests: after about the per-shard p95, send a duplicate to another replica and take the first reply, which costs about 5% extra load. Partial results with a 100 ms deadline. Reduce fan-out via routing, caching hot queries, GC tuning.
  7. Prevention: Track per-shard percentiles and the fan-out-adjusted end-to-end.
  8. Critique: Retries at 3 layers give 3 x 3 x 3 = 27x load on a slow shard, turning a tail problem into a retry storm. Retry at one layer with a retry budget (about 10% of requests), only for idempotent reads, with jitter.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Shards are all slow at once? -> Hedging adds load to a hurting system; the budget caps it and a breaker stops it.
  • Replica counts are 1? -> No second replica to hedge to; that must be solved first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A search cluster at 100 shards met p99 only after hedging at p95 and enforcing a partial-result deadline; blind retries had previously caused a self-inflicted outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: ignores fan-out.
  • Hire: computes 63% and proposes hedging.
  • Strong hire: spots the 27x retry multiplication and proposes a budget.

questions.contextHtml: An ingestion service produces 20,000 small events/s to Kafka. CPU on the broker is at 70% because each send is a separate request with linger.ms = 0. Another team's SLO for these events is "visible to consumers within 500 ms at p99". Two options: A) linger.ms = 20, batch.size 64 KB; B) keep it, add 3 more brokers.
questions.promptHtml: Choose, and explain the trade-off and how you would verify.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Batching is always better for throughput", ignoring the SLO, or "just add brokers" without measuring.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 500 ms end to end? What are payload size and ack settings? Are there other topics with stricter latency? Cost of 3 brokers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed unless the broker is saturating.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Per-request overhead dominates; batching amortises it.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare broker request rate and CPU, producer request-latency-avg, and end-to-end p99 at linger.ms 0, 5, 20.
  5. Reasoning: Batching raises throughput and cuts CPU but adds up to linger.ms of wait per event. 20 ms of added latency against a 500 ms budget is cheap; at 20,000 events/s with 20 ms linger, a batch holds up to about 400 events (or fills at 64 KB sooner). Adding brokers works but is the expensive and slower-to-reverse option.
  6. Fix: Choose A with linger.ms 5 to 20 and compression; keep brokers as is. For any latency-critical topic keep a separate producer config.
  7. Prevention: Track producer batch size and end-to-end lag as SLIs.
  8. Trade-offs: A is a config change, reversible in minutes; B is a capacity decision. If the SLO were 20 ms, A would be wrong.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Events must be ordered per key? -> Batching does not break per-partition order; watch max.in.flight.
  • Traffic drops to 100/s at night? -> Batches fill by timer, so each event pays the full linger; fine within budget.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team batched aggressively for throughput and later found a user-facing notification topic had gained 200 ms of delay; separate producer settings fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks without SLO reasoning.
  • Hire: chooses batching with numbers.
  • Strong hire: separates per-topic configs and defines the verification.

questions.contextHtml: An Android home feed makes 6 sequential API calls at about 120 ms each, 720 ms before anything renders. Target: render under 200 ms with data refreshed in the background. Options: (1) a single aggregate endpoint (BFF); (2) parallelise the 6 calls on the client; (3) cache last-known data locally and render from it first. Some data (balance) must never be shown stale for long.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do and what new problems does it create?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks one option and never mentions invalidation or partial failure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which calls depend on each other? Which fields are user-visible money or safety data? What is the cold-start vs warm-start split? Mobile network quality?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Parallelise independent calls (cheap, client only): about 120 to 150 ms total instead of 720.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Sequential round trips on mobile networks dominate; server time is small.
  4. How I'd verify: Trace per call (client timestamps), simulate 3G/4G latency.
  5. Reasoning: Do less first: aggregate into one BFF call (one connection, one TLS, one trip), then render from a local cache (Room) instantly, and refresh in the background. The BFF adds a service to maintain and a new failure point; use per-section timeouts and partial results.
  6. Fix: BFF with parallel fan-out and a 150 ms budget per optional section; client renders cached data at 0 ms and updates; balance has a short TTL and shows a loading state rather than stale value.
  7. Prevention: Track time-to-first-render by network type; contract tests for the BFF.
  8. Trade-offs: Caching adds an invalidation problem that is hard to undo; the BFF becomes a coordination point between teams. I would not cache money data aggressively.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One section fails in the BFF? -> Return the others with a section-level error and the client keeps the old cached section.
  • Offline? -> Cached render is a bonus; mark staleness.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A feed moved to one BFF call plus local cache; first render dropped from over 700 ms to instant, but a stale balance bug forced per-field TTLs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: names one option.
  • Hire: combines parallel, BFF and cache.
  • Strong hire: addresses staleness classes, partial failure and ownership of the BFF.
